sub: Named after “the scattering winds” sworn by in ayah 1
theme: The Day of Recompense is certain. The surah proves it with oaths, signs in creation and ruined nations, then calls people to flee to Allah and worship Him alone.
story: Revealed in Makkah, in the same period as Sūrah Qāf. The Prophet ﷺ was calling people to Allah and meeting denial, mockery and false accusations, but open persecution had not yet begun.

The Makkans could not agree on what he was: a magician, a poet, a soothsayer, a madman. Reportedly, some split up the roads into Makkah to turn visitors away from him. They mocked the resurrection, asking, “When is this Day?”
The surah answers them. It swears the promise is true, shows how the righteous live, recalls Ibrāhīm’s guests and the nations destroyed, and ends by reminding everyone why they were created.

sections.title: Oaths by winds, clouds, ships, angels: Judgement is real; confused mockers burn
sections.meaning: Allah swears by winds, rain clouds, ships and angels that what you are promised is true and the Judgement will come. By the sky with its paths, the deniers can’t agree on what to say. Cursed are these guessers who mock, “When is that Day?” It is the Day they burn in the Fire.
points: Oaths: scattering winds, laden clouds, easy-sailing ships, angels sharing out affairs
What you are promised is true; the Recompense will happen
By the sky with paths: your talk contradicts itself
Cursed are the heedless guessers who ask, “When?”
The Day they burn: “Taste it, this is what you rushed”
sections.matters: It states the surah’s main claim at once: the Day is certain. The deniers’ own contradictions show they are only guessing, and the answer to their mocking question is the Fire itself.
sections.story: The Makkans kept changing what they called the Prophet ﷺ: magician, poet, soothsayer, madman. Reportedly ayah 8 concerns a group who split up the roads into Makkah to tell visitors these things and turn them away from Islam.
explained: Allah swears by four things: winds that scatter dust, clouds heavy with rain, ships gliding easily (or stars moving in their orbits), and angels who share out provision, rain, hardship and ease by His command. What He swears to: the promise is true, and the Recompense will come.

A second oath, by the sky with its paths: you deniers are in conflicting talk. That contradiction shows it is false, since the truth agrees with itself. Cursed are the guessers, drowning in heedlessness, who mockingly ask when the Day is. The answer: the Day they burn in the Fire and are told, “Taste it.”
teaches: Allah’s oaths by His creation point to His power to bring the promised Day.
Contradiction is a mark of falsehood; the truth agrees with itself.
Talking about the unseen by guesswork is condemned.
Those who mock the Day will taste what they rushed.
sections.hook: Four oaths all ending in -āt: adh-dhāriyāt, al-ḥāmilāt, al-jāriyāt, al-muqassimāt (wind → cloud → ship → angel). Ad-dīn in ayah 6 comes back in the mockers’ question in ayah 12.

sections.title: Night-praying, generous believers win gardens; earth, self and sky confirm the promise
sections.meaning: The righteous will be in gardens and springs, content with what their Lord gives, because they did good before: sleeping little at night, seeking forgiveness before dawn, and giving the needy their right. Then come signs on earth, in yourselves and in the sky. By their Lord, the promise is as real as your speaking.
points: The righteous in gardens and springs; they were doers of good
Little sleep at night; forgiveness sought before dawn
A right in their wealth for the asker and the deprived
Signs on earth and in yourselves: won’t you see?
Provision in the sky; by its Lord, as true as your speech
sections.matters: After the deniers’ Fire comes the other side: what the righteous did to earn Paradise. Then it turns back to the doubters with evidence all around them, and seals it with an oath.
sections.story: It contrasts the believers with the mockers of section 1. One report links ayah 17 to Anṣār who prayed Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ in the Prophet’s ﷺ mosque and then walked on to Qubāʾ.
explained: The muttaqīn will be in gardens and springs, taking what their Lord gives them, fully content. Why? In this life they were muḥsinīn, excellent in worship and good to people. They slept only a little of the night, or hardly let a night pass without prayer, and before dawn they sought forgiveness, feeling their worship still fell short.

They saw a ḥaqq, a right, in their wealth, not a favour: for the one who asks and for the maḥrūm, too dignified to ask. Then look at the earth, at your own body, and at the sky that sends rain. By their Lord, the promise is as certain as the fact that you speak.
teaches: Night prayer and pre-dawn forgiveness mark the people of Paradise.
What you give the needy is their right, not your favour.
Look for the needy who never ask.
Your own body is a sign of Allah’s power to resurrect.
sections.hook: “Wa fī” opens four ayat in a row: in their wealth (19), on earth (20), in yourselves (21), in the sky (22). The first rukūʿ ends at ayah 23.

sections.title: Ibrāhīm’s angel guests don’t eat, then bring news of a learned son
sections.meaning: Allah tells the Prophet ﷺ about Ibrāhīm’s honoured guests. Strangers greet him with peace; he quietly brings a fat calf and invites them to eat. They don’t, and he grows afraid. They reassure him with news of a learned son. His wife cries out: a barren old woman? They reply: your Lord has said so.
points: Honoured guests greet with peace; Ibrāhīm replies, thinking them strangers
He slips away, brings a fat calf: “Won’t you eat?”
They don’t eat; he fears; news of a learned son
His wife cries out, strikes her face: “A barren old woman!”
“So your Lord has said; He is the Wise, the Knowing”
sections.matters: It opens the stories that prove Allah’s word always comes true, as good news and as punishment. The same angels who brought Ibrāhīm joy were on their way to destroy a nation.
sections.story: No specific incident. The guests were angels looking like handsome young men, reportedly three including Jibrīl (other reports say ten or twelve), sent to destroy Lūṭ’s people and told to pass by Ibrāhīm first.
explained: Angels came to Ibrāhīm looking like handsome young men. They said salām; he answered with a fuller salām and thought: strangers. Without announcing anything, he slipped off to his family and came back with a fat calf, the best he had. He set it right in front of them and gently asked, “Won’t you eat?”

Their hands didn’t reach for it. Back then, refusing a host’s food suggested hostility, so he felt afraid. “Don’t be afraid,” they said, and gave news of a learned boy, Isḥāq. His wife Sārah came forward crying out and struck her face in amazement: old and barren! They answered: your Lord decreed it, the Wise, the Knowing.
teaches: Return a greeting with a better one.
Honour guests quickly and with your best, without making a show of it.
Invite gently, “Won’t you eat?”, rather than ordering “Eat”.
Calm the fears of someone who is afraid of you.
Nothing Allah decrees is too hard for Him.
sections.hook: The second rukūʿ opens with “hal atāka ḥadīthu” (24). Salām is said twice in ayah 25. The wife’s cry (29) is answered by two names, al-ḥakīm al-ʿalīm (30).

sections.title: Angels sent to stone Lūṭ’s people; Firʿawn, ʿĀd, Thamūd, Nūḥ also destroyed
sections.meaning: Ibrāhīm asks the angels their mission: marked clay stones for a criminal people. Only one believing household was there, and it was saved; the ruins were left as a sign. Signs too in Firʿawn, drowned with his army; ʿĀd, crushed by a barren wind; Thamūd, struck as they watched; and Nūḥ’s people before them.
points: Your mission? Marked stones of clay for a criminal people
The believers brought out: one household; a sign left behind
Firʿawn calls Mūsā “a magician or a madman”; thrown into the sea
ʿĀd: a barren wind crumbles everything it touches
Thamūd defy their Lord; the blast seizes them as they watch
And Nūḥ’s people before them, defiantly disobedient
sections.matters: Every nation here rejected clear proof and was destroyed, so the promise sworn to in ayah 5 is no empty threat. Each fate is left as a sign for anyone who fears the painful punishment.
sections.story: No specific incident. Ibrāhīm then pleaded for Lūṭ’s people and was told the decree had come (11:74–76). Lūṭ and his family were brought out, except his wife. ʿĀd, Thamūd and Nūḥ’s people had each denied their prophet.
explained: Sensing they were messengers, Ibrāhīm asked their mission. They were sent to Lūṭ’s people, who had committed shirk, denied their messenger and invented a shameful act, to rain clay stones on them, each marked for the one it would hit. Only one household of believers lived there, and it was brought out. The ruined land was left as a sign.

More signs follow. Firʿawn turned away with his army and called Mūsā a magician or a madman, so he was thrown into the sea. ʿĀd were hit by a barren wind that crumbled all it touched. Thamūd were told to enjoy a few days, defied Allah, and were struck while watching. Nūḥ’s people had been destroyed before them all.
teaches: Allah’s punishment is exact: each stone was marked for its target.
Even a single believing household is seen and saved.
Ruined nations are lessons for those who fear Allah.
Armies, power and strength protect no one from Allah.
sections.hook: Juz 27 begins at ayah 31 with “fa-mā khaṭbukum”. “Wa fī” returns from section 2: wa fī mūsā (38), wa fī ʿād (41), wa fī thamūd (43). “Sāḥirun aw majnūn” (39) comes back in 52.

sections.title: Sky built, earth spread, everything in pairs: so flee to Allah alone
sections.meaning: Allah built the sky with strength and expands it, spread out the earth like a bed, and created everything in pairs so people would reflect. So flee to Allah, and set up no other god beside Him. The Prophet ﷺ is a clear warner from Him.
points: The sky built with strength, and We expand it
The earth spread out: how excellent the One who prepared it
Everything created in pairs, so that you remember
Flee to Allah; no other god; I am a clear warner
sections.matters: After the history lesson comes the heart of the invitation. The One who built the sky and made everything in pairs has no partner, so the only safe place to run is to Him.
sections.story: No specific incident. The third rukūʿ begins here, turning from past nations back to signs in creation and a direct call to the listeners.
explained: Bi-ayd means with strength, not hands. Allah raised the sky as a roof and is mūsiʿūn: expanding it, fully able, or generous with provision. He spread the earth like a bed for His creation. And He made everything in pairs, male and female, night and day, land and sea, so you remember that the Maker of pairs is One.

So flee to Allah: from His punishment to His reward, from sin to obedience, from ignorance to knowledge, from heedlessness to remembrance. Running to anything else brings fear; running to Him brings safety. The root of that flight is refusing to set up any other god. Twice comes the line: I am a clear warner to you from Him.
teaches: Everything created comes in pairs; the Creator alone is One.
Whatever you fear, run to Allah.
Leaving shirk is the first step in fleeing to Allah.
Turn from sin, ignorance and heedlessness towards obedience, knowledge and remembrance.
sections.hook: Three creation lines, each opening with its subject: was-samāʾa (47), wal-arḍa (48), wa min kulli shayʾ (49). Ayat 50 and 51 end identically: innī lakum minhu nadhīrun mubīn.

sections.title: Every messenger was called mad; we exist to worship; deniers’ punishment awaits
sections.meaning: Every earlier messenger was called a magician or a madman. Did they pass the words down? No, they share the same arrogance. So turn away, you are not to blame, but keep reminding: it benefits believers. Jinn and mankind exist only to worship Allah, who needs nothing. The wrongdoers’ share of punishment is coming.
points: Every messenger called a magician or madman; a transgressing people
Turn away, you’re not blamed; remind, it benefits believers
Jinn and mankind made to worship; Allah wants no provision
Allah is the Provider, owner of firm strength
A share of punishment like their predecessors’; woe on their Day
sections.matters: It comforts the Prophet ﷺ and states the purpose of every life: to worship Allah. Then the surah ends where it began, with the promised Day, now as a warning instead of an oath.
sections.story: Reportedly, when “turn away from them” (54) came, the Prophet ﷺ was saddened and the Companions feared revelation had stopped and punishment was near. Then ayah 55 came, telling him to keep reminding, and they were relieved.
explained: The Prophet ﷺ is comforted: every earlier nation called its messenger a magician or a madman. They didn’t hand those words down to each other; their hearts were alike in arrogance, so the same words came out. So turn away from the stubborn, since you have delivered the message, but keep reminding. Reminders benefit hearts that have faith.

Allah created jinn and mankind only to worship Him, not because He needs them. He wants no provision or food from them; He is ar-Razzāq, the Provider, full of strength. The wrongdoers will get a dhanūb, a bucketful share of punishment like their predecessors. Let them not rush it: woe to them on their promised Day.
teaches: Mocking those who call to the truth is an old pattern; don’t lose heart.
Keep reminding, even when many don’t listen.
The purpose of your whole life is to worship Allah.
Allah needs nothing from you; you need Him in everything.
A delayed punishment is not a cancelled one.
sections.hook: “Sāḥirun aw majnūn” (39) returns in 52, and tawallā (39) returns as fa-tawalla ʿanhum (54). The surah opens with tūʿadūn (5) and closes with yūʿadūn (60).

groups.text: Allah swears by winds scattering dust, clouds carrying rain, ships sailing easily, and angels sharing out affairs by His command.
What you are promised is true, and the Judgement will certainly happen.
By the sky with its paths: your talk about the Prophet ﷺ contradicts itself, and only the misguided are turned away.
Cursed are the guessers, lost in heedlessness, who mockingly ask when the Day of Judgement is.
It is the Day they burn in the Fire: “Taste it, this is what you wanted hurried.”
The righteous enjoy gardens and springs, taking what their Lord gives, because they did good before.
They slept little at night, sought forgiveness before dawn, and gave the asker and the deprived their right.
The earth holds signs for people of certainty, and so do your own selves. Won’t you see?
Your provision and what you’re promised are in the sky. By its Lord, it is as true as your speaking.
Ibrāhīm’s honoured guests greet him with peace; he returns it and thinks them strangers.
He quietly brings a fat calf, sets it before them, and asks, “Won’t you eat?”
They don’t eat, he grows afraid, and they give news of a learned son. His wife cries out; they say Allah decreed it.
Ibrāhīm asks their mission: to send marked stones of clay on a criminal people.
The believers, one household, were brought out, and the ruins were left as a sign.
Firʿawn rejected Mūsā as a magician or madman, and was thrown into the sea with his army.
ʿĀd were hit by a barren wind that crumbled everything it touched.
Thamūd were told to enjoy a while, defied their Lord, and the blast struck them, unable even to rise.
And Nūḥ’s people before them, a defiantly disobedient people.
Allah built the sky with strength, spread out the earth, and made everything in pairs, so you reflect.
So flee to Allah and set up no other god; the Prophet ﷺ is a clear warner from Him.
Every earlier messenger was called a magician or madman, not by agreement but from shared arrogance.
Turn away from them, you’re not to blame, but keep reminding: it benefits believers.
Jinn and mankind were made to worship Allah. He needs no provision from them; He is the strong Provider.
The wrongdoers’ share of punishment matches their predecessors’. Let them not rush it: woe to them on their Day.

1.explain: Adh-dhāriyāt: the winds that scatter dust. Allah swears by His great creations, full of benefit, that His promise is true.

2.explain: Al-ḥāmilāti wiqrā: the clouds carrying a heavy load of water, which Allah uses to benefit lands and people.

3.explain: Al-jāriyāti yusrā: the ships sailing easily over the water. Or the stars moving smoothly in their orbits, beautifying the sky and guiding travellers.

4.explain: Al-muqassimāti amrā: the angels who share out provision, rain, hardship and ease by Allah’s command, each doing exactly what he was assigned. If ayah 3 means stars, the oaths climb: wind, cloud, stars, angels.

5.explain: This is what the oaths are for: what you are promised, the resurrection with its reward and punishment, is a true promise.

6.explain: Ad-dīn: the Recompense after the reckoning. It will certainly happen, and nothing can push it away.

7.explain: A new oath. Al-ḥubuk: the sky’s paths, like the ripples a breeze makes in sand and water. Or its beauty and perfect build, like finely woven cloth.

8.explain: Qawl mukhtalif: conflicting talk. The Makkans called the Prophet ﷺ a magician, poet, soothsayer or madman, and the Quran magic or old tales. Or it means some believed while others denied.
8.why: Reportedly revealed about al-muqtasimūn: a group who split up the roads into Makkah and agreed what to say about the Prophet ﷺ, so they could turn visitors away from Islam.

9.explain: Yuʾfaku ʿanhu man ufik: only someone already deprived of guidance is turned from the Quran. Or this conflicting talk turns people away, as when they told a would-be believer he was a magician or madman.

10.explain: Qutila al-kharrāṣūn: cursed are the guessers, liars who speak about Allah and the resurrection with no knowledge.

11.explain: Ghamrah: a flood of ignorance and disbelief covering them. Sāhūn: careless and heedless of the Hereafter.

12.explain: They ask, “When is the Day of Recompense?” not to learn, but to doubt, mock and deny it.

13.explain: Yuftanūn: punished and burned over the Fire, the way gold is put into fire.

14.explain: They are told: “Taste your fitnah, your punishment. This is what you demanded be hurried!” It is said to shame them for their mocking.

15.explain: Al-muttaqīn, those who lived with taqwā, are in gardens full of every kind of fruit, with flowing springs.

16.explain: They take what their Lord gives them, fully content, wanting nothing else. Before that, in this life, they were muḥsinīn: worshipping as if they saw Allah, and doing good to people.

17.explain: Hujūʿ is sleep at night. Either they slept only a little and prayed most of the night, or hardly a night passed without some prayer, even just between Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ.
17.why: Reportedly revealed about Anṣār who prayed Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ in the Prophet’s ﷺ mosque, then walked on to Qubāʾ. Another report ties it to the time night prayer was first commanded.

18.explain: Al-asḥār: the last hours before dawn. After praying at night they asked forgiveness, feeling their worship fell short. Allah descends each night in its last third, offering forgiveness to whoever asks.

19.explain: A ḥaqq, a right, in their wealth, not a favour. It is for the sāʾil, who asks, and the maḥrūm: the needy person too dignified to ask, or with no income.

20.explain: Signs on earth for al-mūqinīn, people of certainty: mountains, seas, rivers, trees, plants and animals, all pointing to the Creator’s might.

21.explain: And signs in yourselves: your stages from a drop to a full human, your different languages and colours, every organ in its place. Won’t you see that He can resurrect you?

22.explain: In the sky is your provision: the rain that grows your food. And what you are promised: Paradise, or reward and punishment, written and sent down from Allah.

23.explain: Allah swears by Himself, Lord of sky and earth: it is as true as your own speaking. You never doubt that you speak, so don’t doubt the resurrection.

24.explain: Hal atāka: an opening that signals an important story. The guests were angels, honoured by Allah, and honoured by Ibrāhīm, who served them himself.

25.explain: They said salāman; he replied salāmun, a fuller, lasting greeting. Qawmun munkarūn: strangers. He either said it to himself or asked them who they were.

26.explain: Rāgha: he slipped away quietly, so they wouldn’t stop him, and brought a fat roasted calf, the best food he had.

27.explain: He put it right in front of them and invited them gently: “Won’t you eat?” He didn’t order “Eat”, or make them get up and come to it.

28.explain: Their hands didn’t reach the food. In those days refusing a host’s food signalled hostility, so he felt afraid. They reassured him with news of a learned son, Isḥāq.

29.explain: His wife Sārah came forward with a ṣarrah, a loud cry, struck her face in amazement and said: an old woman, barren even when young, have a child?

30.explain: They answered: this is what your Lord has said. He is al-Ḥakīm, who puts everything in its place, and al-ʿAlīm, who knows all. So accept His decree.

31.explain: Sensing they were messengers sent for something serious, Ibrāhīm asked: “What is your mission?”

32.explain: Sent to a criminal people: Lūṭ’s people, who committed shirk, denied their messenger and did a shameful act no one before them had done.

33.explain: To send down on them stones of ṭīn, clay baked hard in fire.

34.explain: Musawwamah: each stone marked by Allah with the name of the one it would strike. Al-musrifīn: those who went beyond every limit.

35.explain: Before the punishment, Allah brought out every believer living in those towns.

36.explain: Only one household of Muslims was found there: Lūṭ and his family, except his wife, or Lūṭ and his two daughters.

37.explain: Allah left a sign there: their ruined land, turned into a foul, dead sea. Those who fear the painful punishment learn from it and avoid what those people did.

38.explain: Wa fī mūsā: in Mūsā’s story too there is a sign. He came to Firʿawn with sulṭān mubīn: clear proof and plain miracles.

39.explain: Bi-ruknih: with his army and chiefs, who held him up like a pillar. Firʿawn called Mūsā a magician or a madman, even though he knew Mūsā was truthful.

40.explain: Allah seized him and his soldiers and threw them into al-yamm, the sea. Mulīm: blameworthy, for denying the messenger and claiming to be lord.

41.explain: In ʿĀd too is a sign, when they denied Hūd: al-rīḥ al-ʿaqīm, the barren wind that carries no rain and brings no good. A hadith says ʿĀd were destroyed by the westerly wind.

42.explain: It left nothing it came upon, whether people, animals or wealth, except like ramīm: crumbled, rotten remains.

43.explain: Thamūd denied Ṣāliḥ and, after killing the she-camel, were told: “Enjoy yourselves for a while”, which was three days.

44.explain: They arrogantly refused their Lord’s command, so aṣ-ṣāʿiqah, the deadly blast, seized them in broad daylight while they watched it come.

45.explain: They couldn’t even get up, let alone escape, and they had no way to defend themselves.

46.explain: And Nūḥ’s people before all of these: fāsiqīn, defiantly disobedient. They denied Nūḥ and were drowned.

47.explain: Bi-ayd: with strength, not hands. Allah raised the sky as a roof. Mūsiʿūn: We expand it, or We are fully able, or We give provision generously.

48.explain: He spread the earth like a bed, ready for living, farming and travelling. Fa-niʿma al-māhidūn: how excellent the One who prepared it.

49.explain: Zawjayn: pairs. Male and female, sky and earth, night and day, land and sea, light and darkness. So you remember that the Creator of pairs is One.

50.explain: Fa-firrū ilā Allāh: flee from His punishment to His reward, from sin to obedience, from ignorance to knowledge. Running to anything else brings fear; running to Him brings safety.

51.explain: Setting up no other god is the root of fleeing to Allah. The same line, “I am a clear warner to you from Him”, ends both ayah 50 and 51.

52.explain: Comfort for the Prophet ﷺ: every messenger before him was called a magician or a madman, the same words Firʿawn used in ayah 39.

53.explain: Atawāṣaw bih: did they pass these words down to each other? No, they are ṭāghūn, transgressors. Their hearts were alike in arrogance, so their words were alike.

54.explain: Fa-tawalla ʿanhum: turn away from them and don’t let them trouble you. You are not to blame; you have delivered the message.

55.explain: Keep reminding: it benefits hearts that have faith. Some reminders teach what people don’t yet know in detail; others refresh what believers know but have let slip.
55.why: Reportedly, when ayah 54 came, the Prophet ﷺ was saddened and the Companions feared revelation had stopped and punishment had come. Then this ayah came, and they were relieved.

56.explain: Allah created jinn and mankind only to worship Him: to know, love and obey Him. He commanded all of them to; not all choose it, just as a pen sharpened for writing may go unused.

57.explain: Unlike a master who buys a servant to earn for him, Allah wants no provision from them and needs no one to feed Him. They are the ones in need.

58.explain: Ar-Razzāq: the Provider of every creature. Dhū al-quwwah al-matīn: owner of all strength, utterly firm, able even to raise the dead after they have been scattered.

59.explain: Dhanūb: a big bucket drawn in turns at a shared well, so a share. The wrongdoers’ share of punishment will come, like that of ʿĀd, Thamūd and Nūḥ’s people. So don’t rush it.

60.explain: Wayl: woe, a severe punishment, for the disbelievers from their promised Day: the Day of Resurrection, or, in another view, the Day of Badr.
